purpose: Ramucirumab is used to treat certain types of cancer, including stomach cancer, lung cancer, liver cancer, and colorectal cancer. It is often used when other treatments have not worked or have stopped working. It is usually given together with chemotherapy or sometimes on its own.
how_it_works: Your body makes a protein called VEGF that helps tumors grow new blood vessels to feed themselves. Ramucirumab is a special lab-made antibody that blocks the receptor (door) that VEGF uses to signal blood vessel growth. By blocking this door, it cuts off the tumor's blood supply and helps slow or stop the cancer from growing and spreading.
common_side_effects: Low white blood cell counts (which raises infection risk), fatigue and tiredness, loss of appetite, nausea, diarrhea, high blood pressure, swelling in the legs or feet, headache, and rash. Some people may also notice nosebleeds or mouth sores.
warnings: Ramucirumab can cause serious bleeding, including internal bleeding — tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual bleeding or blood in your stool or coughing up blood. It can cause serious high blood pressure, so your blood pressure will be monitored closely. There is a risk of bowel perforation (a hole in the gut), which is a medical emergency. It may slow wound healing, so it is usually stopped before surgery. It can also cause serious infusion reactions during the IV treatment — staff will watch you closely during each dose. Do not use if you are pregnant, as it can harm the baby.
typical_dosing: Ramucirumab is given as an IV infusion (drip through a vein) in a clinic or hospital — you do not take it as a pill at home. The dose and schedule depend on the type of cancer being treated, but a common schedule is once every two weeks. Each infusion usually takes about 60 minutes. Your care team will determine the right dose based on your weight and specific treatment plan.
